endorsements.quote: One solution as suggested by Sweeney C et al. ( 11 ) is to have the chatbot present gentle reminders to users that they are not human and powered by AI to help them understand that they are not receiving therapeutic treatment from a clinician.
Users should also be made aware of certain risks they may be exposed to such as algorithmic bias, inappropriate conversations, unemphatic responses, and limited responses to crises ( 2 , 7 , 12 ).
Second, if an opt out feature is availed, users should have access to a human therapist who can provide them with the necessary care they need.

Additionally, how user information will be gathered, utilized, and protected ( 62 ) should also be disclosed, presented periodically, and made available whenever requested by the user, similar to Woebot and Wysa ( 2 ).
Another solution is to ensure that the training data is representative and inclusive of various populations, especially vulnerable groups ( 54 , 55 ).
Involving mental health associations is crucial for creating AI guidelines for mental health tools.

Third, to reduce bias and TM, users should be involved in the design and developmental stages of these psychological AI chatbots to ensure they are able to support the population they are intended for.

unlisted_practices: Market mental health chatbots honestly, explicitly stating their primary function and purpose and avoiding labels implying therapeutic agents or therapeutic bonds.
Governments should implement policies enabling sufficient oversight and monitoring of mental health chatbots to ensure safe and ethical use.
Inform users when a human intervenes or when they are switched between a clinician and an AI chatbot.
Explicitly tell users that information shared with a chatbot is not covered by patient-provider confidentiality rules.
Allow users to delete their chatbot history and conversations.
Establish international and national guidelines for mental health AI chatbots that promote transparency about risks for vulnerable groups and cultural adaptation.
Involve mental health associations and other stakeholders in regulatory board evaluation committees for mental health AI.

screen.reason: This is a conceptual/ethical perspective paper exploring therapeutic misconception and risks associated with AI-powered mental health chatbots.
